stops.stop: Alexandria, eighteen years old and the school entrusted
stops.date_confidence: attested to his eighteenth year (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.3). Two elements of the pool are corrected here. Eusebius VI.3.1 has him begin because persecution had driven every teacher out, while VI.3.8 says the school was entrusted to him alone by Demetrius: the appointment is the bishop's, not his own initiative, and Eusebius does not reconcile the two. Eusebius VI.3.3 also sets the persecution under the prefect Aquila, whose term in Egypt runs c. 206-211 and cannot be folded into a 203 date; that discrepancy is left open.

stops.stop: Alexandria, the deed Eusebius calls daring
stops.date_confidence: reported and disputed. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.8, is the sole ancient witness; since the early twentieth century a substantial body of scholarship has questioned whether the self-castration happened at all, reading it as hostile tradition Eusebius passed on. Trigg accepts it, Chadwick and McGuckin doubt it. Origen's own Commentary on Matthew rejects a literal reading of the verse. The pool tagged this attested in one lens and reported in another; it is treated here as reported. Year, month and day are ordering devices within c. 206-213.

stops.stop: Alexandria, Heraclas takes the beginners
stops.date_confidence: the delegation to Heraclas is attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.15). The philosophy studies under a teacher named Ammonius and the philosopher's cloak reach Eusebius only inside a passage he quotes from the hostile pagan Porphyry at VI.19.5-8 and then argues against, so they are reported, not attested. The identification of this Ammonius with Ammonius Saccas, later teacher of Plotinus, is disputed and unresolved; Eusebius answers Porphyry by insisting that Ammonius was a Christian raised by Christian parents, which Porphyry denied, and neither claim is independently testable. Year, month and day are ordering devices.

stops.stop: Antioch, the empress's escort
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.21, places the summons in the reign of Severus Alexander and calls Mamaea the mother of the emperor, which rules out anything before March 222; the pool's window of c. 218-222 falls in Elagabalus's reign and is rejected here. Many reconstructions put the Antioch summons at c. 231-232, when Alexander was at Antioch for the Persian campaign, which would place it after the break with Demetrius, whereas Eusebius has him return to Alexandria afterwards. The date given here follows Eusebius's narrative position and is an ordering device, not a finding. Coordinates are the Antioch on the Orontes pin already in use in this corpus.

stops.stop: Alexandria, On First Principles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Alexandrian years (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.24). No modern edition can adjudicate between them. Year, month and day are ordering devices.

stops.stop: Alexandria, the synods and the deposition
stops.date_confidence: reported, not attested, and re-sourced against the pool. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.26, contains no synod, no expulsion and no deposition; its content is the move to Caesarea, Demetrius's death after forty-three years as bishop, and Heraclas's succession. The two Alexandrian synods come from Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 118, echoed by Jerome, and the decrees themselves do not survive. Eusebius's attribution of jealousy to Demetrius is his own partisan reading. Month and day are ordering devices within 231/232.

stops.stop: Tyre, the sixty-ninth year
stops.date_confidence: reported, and the pool's date corrected. Jerome, De Viris Illustribus 54, anchors the death to the reign of Gallus and Volusianus, who were killed in August 253, so the pool's 253/254 overshoots; Wikipedia's biography has him dying less than a year after his release in 251, which would push it earlier. stops.stop: Constantinople, the eleventh anathema
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. The Second Council of Constantinople sat from 5 May to 2 June 553. The fifteen anathemas against Origen popularly attributed to it do not appear in the surviving acts of its eight sessions and no debate on them is recorded there; critical scholarship assigns them to a separate pre-conciliar home synod. Origen's name does appear in the council's eleventh general anathema in most of the manuscript tradition. Wikipedia states the council 'may have anathematized Origen, or it may have only condemned certain heretical teachings which claimed to be derived from Origen'. The existing justinian_i.journey.json stop for this council covers the Three Chapters business only.
